tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: ShowOnboardingRolePicker
tools.description:
Render a clickable role-picker chip row during Cowork onboarding. Call this when asking the user what kind of work they do so they can pick their role and get a matching plugin installed. The role list is hardcoded in the frontend — call with no args.

The call blocks until the user responds. Three resolution paths all land in the tool result: chip click or free-form typed answer → {"role": "Legal"} or {"role": "paralegal"}; X button → {"dismissed": true}. An empty object {} means the user approved without picking a role — treat it like a dismissal. Free-form roles may not match the chip list — search the marketplace with whatever string you get.

Do NOT call this in normal conversation. Only call this when explicitly helping the user set up Cowork for their role/job function.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

schema.name: Skill
schema.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for may add length, unless the part has a budget, as the orientation (`fortress-repo`'s revival part) has. There, new content competes for space with the text already there.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. Do not copy their wording or their style. Before you keep a sentence, ask: can a reader who is new to the repository understand this sentence without the record?

## 4. The principles

`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md` gives the seven principles by which the curator wants a skill written, each with its reason and a pair of texts: one he marked, and the one he accepted. Read it before your first edit. Apply it to every sentence that you write or keep.

## 5. How you work

- Edit the skill files in place. Git keeps the earlier text.
- A comment of the curator marks a problem area. Fix it at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote: `git add -- <paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <paths>`. End every commit message with these two lines, exactly:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

- Do not push. The coordinator pushes.
- Do not touch the review page or its scratch files. The coordinator keeps the page in step.
- Provenance goes only in the skill's `references/sources.md`: one line per change. Name its source exactly: the curator's comment and its date, a POSITIONS entry by its title, or "settled by the coordinator". Do not attribute to the curator a choice that the coordinator made.

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

356	## For Claude: assess all FACTS, rewrite only failing entries
357	
358	The curator requests a **full assessment pass over FACTS**, not only entries written before the writing guidance. Rewrite entries that fail the checks below; leave passing entries intact. This work follows the positions work and precedes Revival consolidation. It is a proposal for the coordinator's existing record process, not an edit of FACTS or the skills.
359	
360	### Why the pass includes newer entries
361	
362	A bounded historical comparison at `origin/main ae2d3dbc5` found:
363	
364	- `ea4d2f1bf`, October 8: ASD-STE100 enters the skill writer's standing brief.
365	- `7b434aae5`, October 13: “Write halfway to ASD-STE100” appears in the coordinator's record-writing part. This is the relevant boundary for FACTS.
366	- `a88e52bf7`, October 13, numbers existing entries. A fact's first appearance with an F-number is not necessarily its creation date.
367	- Older array-bound material, now F-151, is more focused after consolidation.
368	- F-261 and F-262, created October 20 in `36d53bdd6`, are useful examples of focused, scoped writing. Their wording was assessed, not their underlying claims independently re-proved.
369	- F-263 (`5ad4a9957`) and F-264 (`444f37018`) were also created October 20. They mix current behaviour with repair details, counts and historical shorthand, even after changes in the consolidation commit `bd33a2f8b`.
370	
371	This sample supports uneven application of otherwise useful guidance. It does not establish a general failure of ASD-STE100 or prove that later entries are worse. Age is useful provenance, not a rewrite criterion.
372	
373	### Entry schema: meaning before format
374	
375	Retain Markdown and permanent F-identifiers. Refine the existing entry form; do not introduce a database or require every entry to fill repetitive labelled fields.
376	
377	Each entry should communicate:
378	
379	1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
380	2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.
381	3. **Evidence and route to detail.** The supporting test, measurement, source reading or report section. Distinguish observed behaviour from code inspection or an inference. A missing automated test is not itself a defect if other evidence is honestly identified.
382	
383	Keep the source conditions with the claim. Move repair chronology to history and task-specific detail to the cited report. A historical measurement can remain a useful fact if it is explicitly scoped to that measurement; do not mechanically delete every number or past-tense sentence. Link to the owning current count rather than duplicating a count that changes at every landing.
384	
385	A FACTS entry may record an implementation choice made under a default. It must distinguish that fact from a curator-approved ruling. POSITIONS owns the ruling; history owns its origin.
386	
387	### Per-entry assessment rubric
388	
389	Use a temporary assessment table with one row per F-identifier. Mark each criterion **pass**, **fail**, or **unresolved**, with a short reason and a quoted passage for each fail. “Unresolved” means evidence is needed, not that a reviewer may guess.
390	
391	| Criterion | Pass condition |
392	|---|---|
393	| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
394	| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
395	| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
396	| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
397	| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
398	| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |
399	
400	Do not average these into a score that allows good prose to compensate for an unsupported claim. Scope, evidence and consistency failures block acceptance. Comprehension and ownership failures require a wording or organization correction.
401	
402	Assign each entry a disposition:
403	
404	- **Keep:** all applicable checks pass.
405	- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.
406	- **Reorganize:** move detail, merge with an existing owner, or split independently changing claims. Keep conditions and exceptions with their claims.
407	- **Investigate:** support or consistency is unresolved. Resolve the narrow question before approving new wording; do not silently delete the fact.
408	
409	Useful completion measures are assessed entries / total entries, counts by disposition, and unresolved failures by criterion. Every entry must have a disposition; every changed entry must be checked again. Report remaining unresolved items explicitly. Character count is a diagnostic, not an acceptance score.
410	
411	### Run it within the existing process
412	
413	1. Pin the base and list every F-identifier. Divide the assessment using the coordinator's existing bounded chunks. Calibrate on a few contrasting entries, including a concise one and a dense batch-derived one, before expanding.
414	2. Read every entry, following its cited evidence as needed to establish the retained claim. Use bounded report sections and related-entry searches. No automatic rerun of experiments or full transcript archaeology; record a narrow evidence gap when those would be needed.
415	3. Produce the temporary assessment table before rewriting. Do not rewrite passing entries merely to make their surface form uniform.
416	4. Rewrite or reorganize the failing entries using the existing writer pass. Apply the ASD-STE100-inspired register and the scope-preservation rules. Preserve identifiers and use `record.py` with its history and checks. After splits or merges, reconcile incoming references.
417	5. Review changed entries against evidence, then use the existing fresh-reader quiz for consequential distinctions. The reader should know ordinary Fortress concepts but not the original conversation. Distinguish a missing prerequisite from defective wording.
418	6. Recheck affected related entries. Complete the pass with coverage and unresolved-item counts. If main changed during the work, reconcile entries changed since the pinned base rather than overwriting them.
419	7. Only then use the corrected current record as input to Revival consolidation. Do not copy every fact into Revival.
420	
421	This is a full entry assessment with targeted evidence review and selective rewriting, not a fresh scientific verification of the entire repository.
422	
423	### Ownership and minimal instruction changes
424	
425	The present worker skill already says: “Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.” Keep that division of labour.
426	
427	- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
428	- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.
429	- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
430	- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.
431	
432	Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.
433	
434	Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.
435	
436	For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:
437	
438	> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?
439	
440	The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.
441

## For Claude: assess all FACTS, rewrite only failing entries

The curator requests a **full assessment pass over FACTS**, not only entries written before the writing guidance. Rewrite entries that fail the checks below; leave passing entries intact. This work follows the positions work and precedes Revival consolidation. It is a proposal for the coordinator's existing record process, not an edit of FACTS or the skills.

### Why the pass includes newer entries

A bounded historical comparison at `origin/main ae2d3dbc5` found:

- `ea4d2f1bf`, October 8: ASD-STE100 enters the skill writer's standing brief.
- `7b434aae5`, October 13: “Write halfway to ASD-STE100” appears in the coordinator's record-writing part. This is the relevant boundary for FACTS.
- `a88e52bf7`, October 13, numbers existing entries. A fact's first appearance with an F-number is not necessarily its creation date.
- Older array-bound material, now F-151, is more focused after consolidation.
- F-261 and F-262, created October 20 in `36d53bdd6`, are useful examples of focused, scoped writing. Their wording was assessed, not their underlying claims independently re-proved.
- F-263 (`5ad4a9957`) and F-264 (`444f37018`) were also created October 20. They mix current behaviour with repair details, counts and historical shorthand, even after changes in the consolidation commit `bd33a2f8b`.

This sample supports uneven application of otherwise useful guidance. It does not establish a general failure of ASD-STE100 or prove that later entries are worse. Age is useful provenance, not a rewrite criterion.

### Entry schema: meaning before format

Retain Markdown and permanent F-identifiers. Refine the existing entry form; do not introduce a database or require every entry to fill repetitive labelled fields.

Each entry should communicate:

1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.
3. **Evidence and route to detail.** The supporting test, measurement, source reading or report section. Distinguish observed behaviour from code inspection or an inference. A missing automated test is not itself a defect if other evidence is honestly identified.

Keep the source conditions with the claim. Move repair chronology to history and task-specific detail to the cited report. A historical measurement can remain a useful fact if it is explicitly scoped to that measurement; do not mechanically delete every number or past-tense sentence. Link to the owning current count rather than duplicating a count that changes at every landing.

A FACTS entry may record an implementation choice made under a default. It must distinguish that fact from a curator-approved ruling. POSITIONS owns the ruling; history owns its origin.

### Per-entry assessment rubric

Use a temporary assessment table with one row per F-identifier. Mark each criterion **pass**, **fail**, or **unresolved**, with a short reason and a quoted passage for each fail. “Unresolved” means evidence is needed, not that a reviewer may guess.

| Criterion | Pass condition |
|---|---|
| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |

Do not average these into a score that allows good prose to compensate for an unsupported claim. Scope, evidence and consistency failures block acceptance. Comprehension and ownership failures require a wording or organization correction.

Assign each entry a disposition:

- **Keep:** all applicable checks pass.
- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.
- **Reorganize:** move detail, merge with an existing owner, or split independently changing claims. Keep conditions and exceptions with their claims.
- **Investigate:** support or consistency is unresolved. Resolve the narrow question before approving new wording; do not silently delete the fact.

Useful completion measures are assessed entries / total entries, counts by disposition, and unresolved failures by criterion. Every entry must have a disposition; every changed entry must be checked again. Report remaining unresolved items explicitly. Character count is a diagnostic, not an acceptance score.

### Run it within the existing process

1. Pin the base and list every F-identifier. Divide the assessment using the coordinator's existing bounded chunks. Calibrate on a few contrasting entries, including a concise one and a dense batch-derived one, before expanding.
2. Read every entry, following its cited evidence as needed to establish the retained claim. Use bounded report sections and related-entry searches. No automatic rerun of experiments or full transcript archaeology; record a narrow evidence gap when those would be needed.
3. Produce the temporary assessment table before rewriting. Do not rewrite passing entries merely to make their surface form uniform.
4. Rewrite or reorganize the failing entries using the existing writer pass. Apply the ASD-STE100-inspired register and the scope-preservation rules. Preserve identifiers and use `record.py` with its history and checks. After splits or merges, reconcile incoming references.
5. Review changed entries against evidence, then use the existing fresh-reader quiz for consequential distinctions. The reader should know ordinary Fortress concepts but not the original conversation. Distinguish a missing prerequisite from defective wording.
6. Recheck affected related entries. Complete the pass with coverage and unresolved-item counts. If main changed during the work, reconcile entries changed since the pinned base rather than overwriting them.
7. Only then use the corrected current record as input to Revival consolidation. Do not copy every fact into Revival.

This is a full entry assessment with targeted evidence review and selective rewriting, not a fresh scientific verification of the entire repository.

### Ownership and minimal instruction changes

The present worker skill already says: “Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.” Keep that division of labour.

- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.
- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.

Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.

Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:

> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?

The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.

## Review limits

This review sampled Revival and its sources. It did not reread the whole file, audit FACTS or POSITIONS, inspect transcripts, run builds, or test the numerical claims anew. Growth measurements are attributed to the existing scout report.

Its "Built." or "Still to build:" line stays in the entry. It lists no FACTS entries: `P-48+` finds them.

- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.

57:## Reserved points and repairs
58-
59-- A reversible reserved point does not hold the batch. The batch lands with the point's default, and the point goes on the review list.
60-- An output that the base already varies from run to run, with the test's verdict unchanged, is a ledger row.
61-- After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green. Its findings go on the review list, for the batch after. The review runs once in each batch.
62-- A repair after the gate runs the gate again only if it changes what the gate reads (its part in `fortress-repo`).
63-- If the gate over a merged batch is red, do not bisect. Find the cause as a whole, and rework that part in the merged batch. If the gate is still red after its repair, the batch does not land: put it to the curator at once, as a hold.
64-
65-## While it runs
66-
67-- At a boot, read the batch record's sections for the curator, the run's journal (`references/delegating.md`) at the run ID in the check-in file (below), and the times of its agents' transcripts in the session's `subagents/workflows/<run>/`.
68-- From the launch until the run ends, by landing, by stopping or by holding its push for the curator, edit no tracked file in the main tree, the boot note included. content.content:
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**PLAN**
: Working plan, `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`. Its last phases are 3, the checker at zero; 4, the switch-over; 5, microGPT compiles; 6, microGPT fast. These are not the phases of a run (below). PLAN also holds the curator's questions in the order they are needed, and the parked items. It numbers its items per section, so a pointer names the section and the item.

**review queue**
: `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`: numbered items that wait for the curator's word or review. A pointer cites an item by its number.

**default**
: Choice that an agent made and landed without the curator's word. It stands in the tree, and its item in the review queue waits for the curator's review.

**Built.**, **Still to build:**
: State words that end a POSITIONS entry. "Built." means that the decision is in the landed tree. "Still to build:" names the work owed and where it is tracked, such as a PLAN item or a gap-ledger row.

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: C4, the flat program (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a line of the two programs.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the run time), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**count stage**
: Gate's stage that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total, the checker count, counts the errors up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the compiled checker's errors on the interpreter's library, which must reach zero before the switch-over. The gate's distance stage counts them (`explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`), and FACTS holds the current value.

**batch**
: Run of the batch workflow that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.

**rung**
: One task of a batch, with its own worker and worktree. Its brief is its section of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<N>.md`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, run your test on both paths. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

8:- Class (a) holds 7h51m of the workers' 45h02m of Bash wall time (17.5 %), and 6.4 % of their 122h38m of lifetime. Counted only from the calls whose own command line is class (a), with no waits charged to them, it is 4h06m (9.1 % and 3.4 %).
10:- The most that a resident compiler could save by removing that start-up from every class (a) invocation is 2h13m (loops expanded, 2.98 s each): 4.9 % of the Bash wall time and 1.8 % of the lifetime. The hard cap, if class (a) cost nothing at all, is its own 7h51m: 6.4 % of the lifetime (11.6 % if every wait that I could not tie to a run were also class (a)).
11:- Classes (b) and (c), the suites, builds and stages, hold 47.8 % of the Bash wall time, 2.7 times class (a). The commands that the workers type are not where most of the time goes. What runs inside (b) and (c) was not examined.
15:**Data.** 267 transcripts: 162 under `subagents/` and 105 under `subagents/workflows/` of the coordinating session's folder (`/root/.claude/projects/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/`). 145:Only 76 of the 267 agents ran a class (a) command, and 67 of them ran 60 s or more. The (a) share of an agent's Bash wall time has a median of 0 %, p90 of 46 % and a maximum of 96.5 % (an agent that only measured one compiled-transaction cost). The skeptics and the rung workers are where the class sits: 43 % and 29 % of their Bash time, 12 % and 17 % of their lifetime. The twelve agents with the most (a) time hold 4h10m of the 7h51m (53 %); the top three are `rung:V` (0h38m, 26 % of its life
154:| `bin/fortress OneLine.fss` (walk), five runs | 12.667, 3.198, 2.913, 2.785, 2.869 |
158:`OneLine.fss` is in the scratch folder (`startup/`): a component with `export Executable` and `run() = println("hello")`. It printed `hello` and exited 0 each time. The first run is probably cold: the program's own cache entries are written, and the disk cache after the VM's restart is cold. The nine warm runs have a mean of 2.98 s (2.70 to 3.20). The build's stamp equals the caches' stamp, so no build and no library order were needed; I ran neither. The runs wrote only gitignored cache entr
178:| | 2.98 s | 7,992 s (2h13m) | 4.9 % | 1.8 % |
182:So removing the start-up of each command saves at most 1.8 % of the agents' lifetime (4.9 % of their Bash time), and the likelier figure is about 1 %. If a resident process also kept the library loaded and the checker warm, so that class (a) commands cost nothing, the cap is 6.4 % of the lifetime (17.5 % of Bash time), or 11.6 % on the most generous reading of the waits. Half of the class's time is in the 48 calls over 100 s, which are work.
188:- Whether to look inside classes (b) and (c), which hold 47.8 % of the Bash wall time (21h32m): `checker-count`, `distance`, `testQuick`, `testSystem` and the like start JVMs themselves. This report counts only the commands that the workers type. If a resident compiler could serve those, the bound would change by a factor I did not measure. It needs a read of the stage scripts and the ant targets, and the curator's word.

- F-106 **The native-wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that `import java` names, private ones too, but skips constructors, static initializers and every method with a `byte`, a `short` or an array in its parameters or result. A wrapped method with a type that has no Fortress counterpart makes the generator refuse the whole import.** The generator writes the compiled path's Fortress wrappers for such a class. So a helper in `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers`, the Java package that the compiled path's library imports, needs a signature that maps to Fortress, even when it is private, unless the generator skips it. Gap-ledger row 368 records the refusal. Evidence: observed when a private helper with a `Class<?>` parameter broke the rebuild (`compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "The repair round"); the skips read in `FortressMethodAdapter.visitMethod` and `SignatureParser.unsayable`.
- F-107 **Three heaps run the interpreter, and a gated test can pass at two of them and die at the third; a compiled test's run step gets the largest.** `bin/fortress` gives the JVM 256 MB unless `JAVA_FLAGS` is set (gap-ledger row 67: realistic programs exhaust it). +## F-106
+
+> - F-106 **The native-wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that `import java` names, private ones too, but skips constructors, static initializers and every method with a `byte`, a `short` or an array in its parameters or result. A wrapped method with a type that has no Fortress counterpart makes the generator refuse the whole import.** The generator writes the compiled path's Fortress wrappers for such a class. Gap-ledger row 368 records the refusal. Evidence: observed when a private helper with a `Class<?>` parameter broke the rebuild (`compile-ladder/rung-default-rendering/REPORT.md`, "The repair round"); the skips read in `FortressMethodAdapter.visitMethod` and `SignatureParser.unsayable`.
+
+Meaning: one correction, from the assessment. The old title said "every method"; the generator skips `<init>`, `<clinit>` and each method whose descriptor holds `B`, `S` or `[`, in a parameter or in the result (`FortressMethodAdapter.java:215-225`, `SignatureParser.java:45-85`, read again). So the consequence now holds only for a helper that is not skipped. Row 368 and the report's "The repair round" state the same exception.

+- "So a helper...": the old consequence, with the exception. The package is the one that `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:14-20` and `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:13` import.
+- Evidence: the report's "The repair round"; row 368 names `private static boolean hasOwnToString(Class<?> c)` in `nativeHelpers/stringOps.java`.

+> - F-108 **The interpreter's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that is not a property of the program.** Under walk with the JVM's default flags, the order varies from run to run. The runs did not test the three flags one at a time. The harness reads only that the `XXX` test fails, not the order. If an output comparison sees the order move, it cites gap-ledger row 430, which records this order. +## F-234
+
+> - F-234 **A Fortress command that a worker runs on its own starts a fresh JVM, and that start costs too little to pay for a resident compiler.** A resident compiler is a background JVM that serves Fortress commands, as Scala 2's `fsc` did. The suites already run each suite in one JVM, and the harness runs each test inside it. Only a compiled test's run step and a `.sh` test, such as `tests/concurrentPrinting.sh`, start another process. The one-off commands took at most 6.4 % of the workers' whole running time, and their start-up at most 1.8 % (P-150: no resident compiler is built). Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/fresh-jvm-commands.md`, "Summary" and "What a resident compiler could save, at most".

### F1, a defect, fixed in `deabd50f6` (settled)

`openWhereSizes` bounded each opened type by its variable's bounds, at the trait's arguments, but left the variable itself unopened inside them.

The rung's `whereSizes` now reads the clause's constraints into those bounds. A constraint that names its own variable, `where [\E\] { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`, is the shape of the team's own commented clauses: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1207`, `T extends Array[\T,E,I\]`, and `Library/SkipList.fss:105`, `SelfType extends InternalNodeHelper[\SelfType,...\]`. With such a constraint, a call that opens the trait stopped the checker. The binding form, `where [\E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]\]`, had failed the same way since climb batch 17's rung A.

    old-fortress.sh ... typecheck SkFBoundedOpen771.fss    (the base)
        - [\E extends CompilerAlgebra.StandardTotalOrder[\E\]\]CBox[\E\]->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type AnyC.
    bin/fortress typecheck SkFBoundedOpen771.fss           (the rung's head)
        SkFBoundedOpen771.fss:8:7-9:
        E is not in the kind env [][][]
    old-fortress.sh ... typecheck SkFBoundedBindOpen771.fss (the base; the head the same)
        E is not in the kind env [][][]

The text accepts the call. A constraint's trait references "may include naked type variables", and "A where clause may include mutually recursive constraints" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:351-352`, `:362`). A listed type holds "at every value of" its where-clause variable (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:236-243`). Row 771's build line says the opened type "carries" the constraint.

The ways I considered:

1. Substitute the opened variables into the bounds before registering them. This is the move the rung's own extender check makes with its inference variables, through `atArgs`.
2. Drop a bound that names a where-clause variable. That keeps the refusal of a call the text accepts.
3. Read only constraints that name no variable into `whereSizes`. That narrows row 771's build.

I took the first way. It is in `openWhereSizes`, a declaration the section gives the rung.

### F5, a note: type where-clause variables of functions and methods

Both paths refuse a function's or a method's type `where`-clause variable at name binding, on the base and on the head (`SkTypeVar749`, `SkTypeVarMethod`): 'E is undefined.' P-151 builds only the forms the team wrote, and the team wrote type where-clause variables only on `comprises` clauses (`Library/SkipList.fss:103-106`, `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/ParametricTree0.fss:30-31`). So this is no gap of the rung's, and I added no row.

It follows that the type branch of the rung's `whereVars` (`STypesUtil.scala:202-203`) is not reached today. It changes nothing, and I left it in place.

## 1. What changed and why

All five rows are built, in the order the section gives.

- **Row 748.** `getCandidatesForMethod` (`Functionals.scala:973-1029`) now drops a candidate whose where clause constrains its trait's or object's static parameter, where the receiver's static argument breaks the constraint.
  - The dropped candidate is not applicable, so another overload is chosen.
  - The methods come instantiated at the receiver. The argument for the trait's parameter is read off the instantiated method's self type, at the position that parameter has in its original's self type. `SelfParamDisambiguator.scala:56-81` builds both from the declaration's static parameters, in order.
  - When every candidate is dropped, the call is refused: "Method Holder[\String\].showIt is not applicable: its where clause requires String to extend Shows."
  - The fold of a functional method's lifted arrow (`STypesUtil.scala:212-221`) is kept.
  - Both callers of `getCandidatesForMethod` get the check: the subscript (`Functionals.scala:1100`) and the method invocation (`:1129`).
- **Row 749.** `makeArrowFromFunctional` (`STypesUtil.scala:195-221`) binds the where clause's own type, `nat` and `int` variables as static parameters of the arrow, after the declared ones, so the call infers them.
  - That alone did not build the row. The arrow `[\U extends Object X[\n\], V extends Object Y[\n\], nat n\](U, V)->String` was still "not applicable to an argument of type (O, P)".
  - The cause is in the solver (`Formula.scala:644-652` at the base). It fixes `U` and `V` from their lower bounds, then finds the size constraint `O <: X[\$n\]` left over and gives up. Its own comment says so: "TODO: We can solve more constraints if we iterate 1), 2) 3) until we hit a fixed point" (`Formula.scala:578`, the team's line; `:441` at `a874948ac`).
  - `Formula.slv` now solves, once, what the type variables' solutions leave when that is sizes alone (`Formula.scala:649-656`). The retry runs only where the first attempt failed, so no call accepted before changes its solution.
  - `GenericFnWithExcludes.fss:44`, `g(O, P)` with `P` a `Y[\2\]`, stays refused: no `n` meets both constraints.
- **Row 750.** The trait-type case of `TypeWellFormedChecker.walk` (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:245-275`) checks the declaration's own trait constraints on its static parameters at the type's static arguments, with the bound's message.
  - The constructor calls `Wrap[\String\]("s")` and `Wrap("s")` (no static argument) are refused through this case, at the call's type: "Ill-formed type: Wrap[\String\] The static argument String does not satisfy the corresponding bound Shows.", at `XXXWhereConstraintTypeUseChecker.fss:14:27-42`.
  - They are not refused through the constructor's arrow, whose where clause (`STypesUtil.scala:178-181`) is not read at a call.
- **Row 753.** `checkDeclComprises` (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala:318-333`) gives each type where-clause variable's inference variable its bounds.
  - The bounds are a conjunct of the formula that `comprisesContains` solves (`:422-438`), passed down through `isEligibleToExtend` and `everyKnownSubtypeListed`.
  - `object NBox[\E extends Object\](item: E) extends AnyNumBox` is refused; `NBox[\E extends Number\]` is taken.
- **Row 771.** `whereSizes` (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:856-882`) bounds a type where-clause variable by its binding and by each trait constraint of the clause on it.
  - So `openWhereSizes`, unchanged, bounds the opened type by both.
  - The extender check of row 753 reads the same bounds (`XXXComprisesWhereConstraintExtenderChecker`).
- **Specification.** Appendix I's entry "The traits that extend a closed trait": its clauses on rows 771 and 753 are revised in the revision form, with the dates (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1486-1501`). The specification build ended in BUILD SUCCESSFUL twice, with no undefined reference.

One hole remains: a static argument written at a top-level call is not checked against a folded bound, so `g[\String\]("s")` is accepted where `g("s")` is refused (gap-ledger row 470). F-256 holds where the checker reads the constraints at a dotted call, at a type's use and at a `comprises` clause. The library edits that landed with this reading are F-242's (the generic `distribute` and the method conditions of `SUM`'s fusion pairs) and F-85's (the identities' `cast` and the typed `embiggen`). It refuses that type where another type is declared, and it gives two values two types. It also refuses the shape of Amin and Tate's 2016 unsoundness example, where such a value would prove a subtype relation that does not hold. It takes the return type only if exactly one api declaration of the name matches. With none or several, it takes none, and the declaration keeps its elisions. One hole remains: a static argument written at a top-level call is not checked against a folded bound, so `g[\String\]("s")` is accepted where `g("s")` is refused (gap-ledger row 470). F-256 holds where the checker reads the constraints at a dotted call, at a type's use and at a `comprises` clause. The library edits that landed with this reading are F-242's (the generic `distribute` and the method conditions of `SUM`'s fusion pairs) and F-85's (the identities' `cast` and the typed `embiggen`). Tests: `compiler_tests/WhereBoundMethodChecker`, `XXXWhereBoundFunctionCall`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-library-distribute/REPORT.md` section 1.
2	- F-251 **A type `where`-clause variable of a `comprises` clause is opened at a call, as a size is, and `AnyList`'s clause is live.** To open a variable is to give it a fresh type of its own for the call, as the compiled checker already does for a listed type's `nat` and `int` sizes (F-146). So the checker gives an argument whose trait lists `Box[\E\] where [\E\]` a fresh type for the call, bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints on it (F-256). It refuses that type where another type is declared, and it gives two values two types. It also refuses the shape of Amin and Tate's 2016 unsoundness example, where such a value would prove a subtype relation that does not hold. It does not open such a trait where it reaches it as a parent (gap-ledger row 752). Walk binds the variable as a symbolic type at load. On the rung's own tree, `AnyList`'s `addLeft`, `addRight` and the comprehension's unwrap, respelled, took the distance from 49 to 45 (gap-ledger row 636's four sites); the count, and walk's element types, did not change. Tests: `OpenTypeChecker`, `XXXOpenTypeEscapeChecker`, `XXXOpenTypeTwoChecker`, `XXXOpenTypeBoundEvidenceChecker`, `OpenTypeWalk`, `AnyListElementTypeWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-anylist-comprises/REPORT.md`.
3	- F-254 **In the compiled checker, a function or method that leaves out its return type takes it from the exported api's declaration that has its own parameter types.** `ApiTypeExtractor` compares the parameter types as the export check does (`ExportChecker.equalTypes`), and a parameter that the function leaves untyped matches any type. It takes the return type only if exactly one api declaration of the name matches. With none or several, it takes none, and the declaration keeps its elisions. So the choice does not depend on the JVM's identity-hash order of the declarations, and no output of the count or distance stage is known to move with that order (F-232): `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:130` is out of both. Evidence: read in `scala_src/typechecker/ApiTypeExtractor.scala:77-126` and `:193-209`. Tests: `OmittedReturnTypeFromApi`, `OmittedMethodReturnTypeFromApi`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-four-rows/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 5.
4	- F-255 **The compiled checker reads conditional extension in its subtype relation: a trait or object that extends a type under a `where` clause of trait constraints only is a subtype of that type exactly where the constraints hold.** The `extends` entry itself, the value parameters and the members are checked with the constraints holding. The static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses and its other `extends` entries are checked without them. The disambiguator drops every trait's and object's `throws` clause and contract, so these are not checked at all (gap-ledger row 781). A clause that binds a variable, or that holds a constraint that is not a trait constraint, is read as before. Limits: a member checked under the condition stays callable where the condition fails (row 773), and walk and the compiled run time read the extension at every instance (row 774). Other readers of the `extends` clause in the checker also read the parent at every instance, for example the inherited `excludes` clauses and the ancestors that the overloading checker sees; no ledger row holds them (report section 10). In the library, `List` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`. On the rung's own tree, against climb batch 17's gate, this cleared the site `FortressLibrary.fss:2063` and added none. Tests: `compiler_tests/CondExtendChecker`, `XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker`, `XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker`, `XXXCondExtendExcludesChecker`, `XXXCondExtendComprisesChecker`, `XXXCondExtendParamBoundChecker`, `XXXCondExtendExcludesWhereChecker`, `CondExtendInheritedMember` (a type that inherits through a conditional parent compiles: the code generator's analyzer reads the parent at every instance), `tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md`, sections 1, 6 and 10.
5	- F-256 **The compiled checker checks a `where` clause's trait constraints where they apply.** At a dotted call, a candidate whose `where` clause constrains its trait's or object's static parameter is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the constraint ('Method Holder[\String\].showIt is not applicable: its where clause requires String to extend Shows.'). If a function's or method's `where` clause has a trait constraint, the clause's `nat` and `int` variables become static parameters of the function's arrow, inferred at the call. So a constraint whose bound names such a variable is met where some value of it meets every constraint. When the type variables' solutions leave only size constraints, the solver tries once more to solve them. Both paths refuse a function's or method's type `where`-clause variable at name binding ('E is undefined.'), so this inference never reaches one. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, with the bound's message, also at a constructor call through the call's type. A type `where`-clause variable of a `comprises` clause is bounded by its binding and by the clause's constraints on it, where it is opened and in the check of an extender. In a bound that names the variable itself, as `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]` does, the opened type stands for the variable. Not read: a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable, at a dotted call or at a type's use; a static argument written at a top-level call (gap-ledger row 470). Walk still runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777), and reads a `comprises` clause's `where`-clause variable for the same name in another declaration's bound (row 778). These checks moved no site of the count or the distance (F-53 holds the current values). Tests: `XXXWhereBoundDottedCallChecker`, `WhereVariableBoundCallChecker`, `XXXWhereConstraintTypeUseChecker`, `XXXWhereConstraintExtendsChecker`, `XXXComprisesWhereBoundExtenderChecker`, `OpenTypeWhereConstraintChecker`, `XXXComprisesWhereConstraintExtenderChecker`, `OpenTypeWhereSelfBoundChecker`. Detail: `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-where-checks/REPORT.md`, sections 1 and 6, and `SKEPTIC.md` beside it.
6	- F-99 **The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file for the two suites, not in the calling shell.** `build.xml`'s `fastTrack` macro, which runs `testFast`, and its `systemShard` macro, which runs `testSystem`, set `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` (P-125). Without the pin, the tests would take the caller's count: half the CPUs if it is unset, or 1 under `env.sh`. The gate's other runners, which `env.sh` sets up, run at one thread (F-203). `fastTrack` also pins `JAVA_FLAGS` to `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, because a compiled test's run step takes its heap and stacks from it. With the JVM's default 1 MB stacks at four threads, `library_tests/TimingRungT` overflowed a thread's stack in 8 of 12 runs (gap-ledger row 640). Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 6.
7	- F-100 **`ant compileAll` deletes the caches folder, the linker's untracked `global.map` with it, when the implementation changed, and keeps it otherwise.** It compares the folder's `implementation.stamp` with the new build's. After a deletion, `fortress run` dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32` until the library order refills the five library jars, in about two minutes (the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`). Two other things clear the caches: `ant cleanCache`, whatever the stamp, and `Shell.resetRepository`, which `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` call unless `fortress.junit.reset` is false, as `testFast` sets it. A `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler does not clear them. The linker writes a missing `global.map` again, empty. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 2.
8	- F-101 **`harness-one.sh` keeps its Fortress cache between calls.** The script is `compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh`, and its cache is the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It reuses the cache while the built implementation and the Fortress sources on the source path are those that filled it. `COLD_CACHE=1` empties it first. Detail: `coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` sections 1 and 4.
9	- F-102 **An `XXX*.fss` in the interpreter corpus is a gated expected-failure test.** `SystemJUTest` marks a file of `ProjectFortress/tests/` whose name starts with `XXX` as one that must fail, and the suite goes red when it passes. Such a test needs a `.test` file only to name a refusal at load, as any program of `tests/` does (F-29: walk's load check and its `load_exception_contains` key). An `XXX` test that imports api pairs takes them from `ProjectFortress/test_library/`, so it needs no new api folder. The compiled corpora's rule differs (F-103). Source: `FileTests.java:780-782` and `:394-412`; the `fortress-repo` skill's `tests-writing.md`, "How `XXX` works".
10	- F-103 **The `XXX` expected-failure mechanism in `compiler_tests/` and `library_tests/` cannot express, in one `.test` file, a program that compiles and then fails at run time.** The `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name makes every command that the file drives a must-fail. So such a defect needs two `.test` files over one component: a plain-named file that drives `link`, and an `XXX` file that drives `run` (the `fortress-repo` skill's `tests-writing.md`, "Writing an `XXX` test"). A compile-stage failure needs one `XXX` compile test. If that test's program compiles, the test is red: "Saw wrong failure", with a `compile_err_contains` key. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tryatomic/REPORT.md`, "The measured defect, and its home".
11	- F-104 **A thrown `CompilerError` takes a third path through the test harness, the exception stream, keyed on the component that `tests=` names, with check keys `compile_exception_*`.** The harness checks three streams of a command: its output, its error output and a thrown exception. `Shell` does not catch a `CompilerError` from the code generator, such as its `sayWhat` refusal of a construct that it cannot compile. So the harness reads it as an exception of the component that the `.test` file's `tests=` line names. If that component's name holds `XXX`, a link or compile exception is green whatever the `.test` file is called; only an unmet key of that command makes it red. A `compile_exception_contains` key pins the refusal's text, so the test turns red when the refusal goes away or changes. Detail: `compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/REPAIR-review.md` section 2.
12	- F-203 **`explorations/experiment/env.sh` sets up a shell for the gate's runners, and takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from its own place in the tree.** It sets the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1` and `JAVA_FLAGS`, and unsets `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. It deletes a `/tmp/fortress*rats` parser folder only if nothing in it was written for an hour and every running `java` process started after its last write, so sourcing it does not break a live run. The ladder regression's scripts source it: `compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh` and its copy in `baseline-2026-09-19/`, `repair-r1-atomic-static/run-subset.sh` and `baseline-2026-09-19/microgpt-phase.sh`. `experiment/setup.sh` sources it too. The count stage's and the distance stage's `run.sh` do not: their headers tell the caller to source it first. A worker sets up each call by the `fortress-repo` skill's lines instead (`build-and-caches.md`, "Setting up each call"). Evidence: read in the scripts; the deletion rule also in `coordinator/process-engineering/build-efficiency.md` section 4.
